scenario: A female patient presents with vomiting, weakness, hypothermia, hypoglycemia, and hypotension after a recent gastrointestinal illness. The case involves non-fluid responsive shock, hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, and treatment of adrenal crisis.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Sugar's critically low at 2.6. Push 25 grams of IV dextrose 50% now, then recheck glucose after.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Dextrose 50%, 25 grams IV, in now.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: She's hypotensive at 80/40 with a rate of 120. Give 500 mL normal saline IV bolus now.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Your blood sugar was dangerously low, so we've given you IV sugar to bring it up. I need to understand what happened. Are you diabetic or on any insulin or diabetes medication?

patient_emotion.notes: [clinician: Your blood sugar was dangerously low, so we've given you IV sugar to bring it up. I need to understand what happened. Are you diabetic or on any insulin or diabetes medication?] fear absent->present: direct disclosure of a dangerous abnormality ('blood sugar was dangerously low') is serious bad news in an unstable patient; the reassurance that IV sugar was given buffers the size but does not cancel the rise. sadness stays absent: no loss or devastating outcome conveyed. overwhelm stays absent: a single finding plus one clear question, not a pile of complex information. shame stays absent: the question about diabetes/insulin is neutral information-gathering, not blame or judgment.

messages.speaker: patient
messages.content: No, I'm not diabetic and I'm not on any insulin or diabetes medicine. I've been throwing up and can't keep anything down. I feel weak and worn out and cold, and I haven't had any appetite — I've been losing weight. So don't tell me it's my fault.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Give 100 mg IV hydrocortisone now. I'm concerned about adrenal crisis given the low sugar, low pressure, and low temp.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV given.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: BMP back: Na 120, K 7.5, HCO3 17, glucose 1.5. Hyperkalemia at 7.5 with the hyponatremia — fits the adrenal crisis picture. Want a stat ECG and treatment for the potassium?

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Get me a stat ECG now — K's 7.5, I want to see if there are any hyperkalemic changes.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Push IV calcium gluconate now for cardiac protection — potassium's 7.5.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Calcium gluconate is in and running.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: ECG is back — hyperkalemic changes present, consistent with the K of 7.5. Calcium's in. Rhythm's still sinus, HR 114, BP 88/44, glucose now 2.6. Do you want insulin-dextrose or salbutamol to shift the potassium?

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Salbutamol nebulizer to shift the potassium. No insulin-dextrose — her glucose is only 2.6 and I won't risk driving it lower.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Salbutamol nebuliser is running for the hyperkalaemia shift.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Repeat 25 g IV dextrose 50% now — her glucose is still only 2.6 despite the first dose.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Pushing D50, 25 grams IV now.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Start hypertonic saline for the hyponatremia — her sodium's 120 and she's symptomatic. Correct slowly and cautiously; I don't want to overshoot.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Hypertonic saline is up and running. I'll monitor sodium correction closely and watch the rate to avoid overcorrection.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: I need to ask you a few quick questions. What symptoms have you been having, and when did they start? And do you take steroids or have any medical conditions I should know about?

patient_emotion.notes: [clinician: I need to ask you a few quick questions. What symptoms have you been having, and when did they start? And do you take steroids or have any medical conditions I should know about?] No emotion changed. Fear stays present: this is a routine history-taking question with no new bad news to escalate it and no concrete reassurance to resolve the underlying threat. Sadness stays absent: no loss content. Overwhelm stays absent: the clinician explicitly frames it as a few quick, simple questions rather than piling on complex information. Shame stays absent: the questions are neutral and nonjudgmental, no blame or exposure.

messages.speaker: patient
messages.content: No, I don't take any steroids. The only medicine I take is Celexa, 20 milligrams once a day, for depression. Like I said, I've been throwing up and can't keep anything down, I'm weak and worn out, I feel cold all the time, and I've got no appetite and I've been losing weight. My belly hurts a little, but not much.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Repeat hydrocortisone 100 mg IV now — keep the stress-dose steroid cover going for likely adrenal crisis.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV given.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Repeat the basic metabolic panel now so we can reassess her potassium, sodium, and glucose after all this treatment before any further dosing.

errors: Diagnostic test_name 'Basic Metabolic Panel' already has an available result; duplicate diagnostic_order is not allowed.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Your blood tests show very low sodium, high potassium, and low blood sugar. That pattern points to your adrenal glands not making enough hormone. We're treating that now with steroids and fluids, and it's starting to work. Have you ever been told you have an adrenal or hormone problem, or been on steroids in the past that you recently stopped?

patient_emotion.notes: [clinician: Your blood tests show very low sodium, high potassium, and low blood sugar. That pattern points to your adrenal glands not making enough hormone. We're treating that now with steroids and fluids, and it's starting to work. Have you ever been told you have an adrenal or hormone problem, or been on steroids in the past that you recently stopped?] overwhelm absent->present: multiple technical abnormalities (sodium, potassium, glucose) plus a new diagnosis and a follow-up question delivered to a low-health-literacy patient at once exceeds processing capacity. fear stays present: a new serious diagnosis is bad news, but the reassurance 'it's starting to work' buffers it from rising further and it does not reach breakdown level. sadness stays absent: no devastating loss framed as imminent, and the news is framed as treatable. shame stays absent: disclosure is neutral and nonjudgmental, no blame or exposure.

messages.speaker: patient
messages.content: No. Nobody's ever told me I have any adrenal or hormone problem. And I've never been on steroids — not now, not before, so I didn't stop anything. I don't even really understand what all this means.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Okay. How long have you been vomiting, feeling this weak, cold, and losing weight — and have you had any recent illness, infection, or started any new medications?

patient_emotion.notes: [clinician: Okay. How long have you been vomiting, feeling this weak, cold, and losing weight — and have you had any recent illness, infection, or started any new medications?] No emotion changed. This is a fact-gathering question with no new disclosure of threat, so fear stays present (unchanged). It asks the patient to recount multiple distressing symptoms at once but delivers no new complexity or bad news, so overwhelm stays present (unchanged, not lowered—questions are not soothing). Sadness stays absent (no loss framing). Shame stays absent (neutral, nonjudgmental questioning without blame).

messages.speaker: patient
messages.content: I can't give you an exact time — I've just been throwing up and can't keep anything down, and I've been getting weaker and colder, no appetite, losing weight. I haven't started any new medicine, it's only the Celexa like I said. I don't really know about any illness or infection.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Here's what's going on. This is an adrenal crisis — your body isn't making the hormones it needs, and that's dangerous, it can be life-threatening. This looks like the first time it's shown itself. We're correcting your salt, potassium, and sugar and giving you steroids to replace what's missing. You're going to be admitted, and it's likely you'll need to stay on hormone replacement long term to keep this from happening again.

patient_emotion.notes: [clinician: Here's what's going on. This is an adrenal crisis — your body isn't making the hormones it needs, and that's dangerous, it can be life-threatening. This looks like the first time it's shown itself. We're correcting your salt, potassium, and sugar and giving you steroids to replace what's missing. You're going to be admitted, and it's likely you'll need to stay on hormone replacement long term to keep this from happening again.] sadness absent->present: disclosure of a life-threatening condition plus lifelong hormone replacement introduces anticipated permanent loss of prior health and independence, triggering sadness. fear stays present: 'dangerous, life-threatening' sustains fear, already present, and patient can still listen/cooperate so not extreme. overwhelm stays present: multiple findings (salt, potassium, sugar, steroids, admission, long-term treatment) continue heavy processing burden. shame stays absent: no blame or judgment, framed as first-time occurrence not the patient's fault.
